summary:
Trans visitors to Tennessee stand under the United States federal framework as well as state law. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed these restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry, while trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. TSA screening can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, and several foreign governments have issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules.

Tennessee's Adult Entertainment Act of 2023 (SB 3/HB 9) criminalises "adult cabaret entertainment", a definition that expressly includes "male or female impersonators", performed on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony carrying 1 to 6 years and fines to $3,000. A trans visitor who performs, or who is perceived as performing, within that definition faces repeat-offence felony exposure after a single prior conviction.

The Act survived federal challenge on procedural grounds, and in 2026 the Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to it, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the 2023 statute in place. A separate suit over the law remains ongoing.

Violence risk is documented at a level well above the national picture. A July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams Institute data records Tennessee's killing rate of trans women at 7.8 per 100,000 per year, based on 10 recorded deaths between 2008 and 2025 and treated as an undercount floor rather than a total. The same analysis places Tennessee in the "Worst Laws Passed" tier of states.

Custody is hazardous. In April 2024 the Tennessee State Legislature passed a bill banning gender-affirming care for Tennessee inmates. Under the 2026 Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act, transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons according to sex assigned at birth, and the same Act bans trans women from women's shelters, removing an access point for a visitor who has no other accommodation.
tangentialFactors:
Tennessee sits within a wider pattern of sub-national restriction rather than an isolated case. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia having no such ban, and some states making trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and drag restrictions of the kind Tennessee enacted have been adopted elsewhere.

National assessments have moved against Tennessee's neighbours as well. A July 2026 risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends. Federal measures of this kind have been blocked or enjoined in some instances, but the injunction record does not reach Tennessee's own statute, whose federal challenge failed.

The comparison worth holding onto is that the documented killing rate in Tennessee is stated per capita against a national baseline in which trans homicide is already undercounted; the figure of 7.8 per 100,000 per year is presented as a floor. Civil-rights attorneys elsewhere have described comparable state measures as precedent-setting, and rights groups have characterised the 2026 Kansas document law as a template other legislatures are expected to copy.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tennessee live under the same Adult Entertainment Act that binds a visitor. The statute's reach on public property and anywhere a child could be present constrains drag and impersonation performance in the state year-round, and the felony tier attaches on a second violation regardless of who is charged.

For incarcerated trans residents, the April 2024 statute banning gender-affirming care applies alongside the 2026 birth-sex placement mandate, so prison assignment follows sex assigned at birth for the state prison population as a whole. Trans women residents also lose access to women's shelters under the same 2026 Act, which affects people with no alternative housing rather than only those passing through.

Tennessee is graded in the "Worst Laws Passed" tier of a national state-by-state analysis, and the recorded killing rate for trans women of 7.8 per 100,000 per year is compiled from state death records over 2008 to 2025, a period in which advocacy datasets treat the count as an undercount floor.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the ongoing separate suit over the Adult Entertainment Act has produced relief since the Supreme Court declined the earlier petitions is unresolved in the sources and should be checked against a current court docket before publication.

The sources do not state whether any provision of the 2026 Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act has been enjoined, and they do not say whether the shelter ban applies to emergency shelters operated by municipalities as well as private providers. Both points are unresolved.

No source in this inventory addresses Tennessee's rules on changing sex markers on state driver's licences or birth certificates, nor any state-level bathroom or facilities restriction binding a visitor in ordinary public accommodation. Those questions are not sourced here and are not answered by the federal document rules alone.

The April 2024 inmate-care bill and the 2026 Act are cited through a state-rights reference article rather than through the enrolled statutes themselves; the operative text and section numbers should be verified against the Tennessee Code before the penalties and placement rules are quoted as settled.
